gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.anglerfi: Field observation records a predatory lure used to draw closer targets into range.
The species holds position for long intervals and advances only when a target is close enough.
Bottom survey confirms a seabed-oriented species that navigates by touch and current cues.
Behavior is opportunistic and efficient, with a clear preference for sheltered routes and debris fields.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.creeporp: The specimen remains visually quiet while storing charge, which makes its threat level easy to underestimate.
When stimulated, it releases stored force abruptly and leaves little time for a second response.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.donutfis: Distinctive ring-shaped specimen with calm movement and no aggressive response during initial contact.
Feeding notes classify it as a low-risk grazer that remains predictable under routine observation.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.electrof: Ambient water registers charge before direct visual contact, indicating a strongly reactive species.
The specimen feeds on motion and resistance, and it keeps nearby currents disturbed even at rest.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.giant_ab: Titan-class trench specimen. Its emergence disrupts local current structure across a wide area.
The body is segmented and heavily mobile, so field work should prioritize distance and exit routes.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.giant_oc: A single limb sample is enough to confirm titan-scale reach before the full body is visible.
Observed behaviors are probing, gripping, and retrieval, all consistent with a much larger host organism.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.gloomgaz: Low-light predator that reduces visible contrast in the surrounding water as it approaches.
It waits motionless in dim areas and relies on patient ambush rather than pursuit.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.helicopr: Ancient predatory specimen with a spiral jaw structure and no sign of behavioral moderation.
The jaw assembly is the primary hazard and appears specialized for forceful contact at close range.
Cold-water glider with motion tuned to low temperatures and minimal surface disturbance.
Performance drops outside chilled currents, so temperature is a key environmental variable.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.lighting: Electrically active worm-like specimen that announces itself through a clear voltage signature.
The species converts ambient charge into sustained motion and remains active around conductive water.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.manta_ra: Large gliding specimen that maintains broad, level passes through open water.
The body plan favors pressure tolerance and efficient travel over acceleration or aggression.
Armed survey specimen. It tests the environment before committing to a route.
Behavior is cautious and methodical, with strong preference for cover, texture, and timing.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.oxygen_b: Utility species that improves local water conditions rather than competing with nearby life.
Metabolic output appears to create usable oxygen, making the species valuable in confined systems.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.radioane: Signal-emitting reef organism that alters nearby water behavior before direct contact.
It appears to consume and emit the same energy class, keeping the immediate area in a constant pulse state.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.red_jell: Visually prominent stinging specimen. Light output is not a reliable indicator of safety.
Disturbance triggers an immediate defensive strike, so close handling should be minimized.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.ringfish: Loop-shaped herbivore that turns in regular arcs and keeps to steady water.
Observed behavior is calm and predictable, with little deviation from a slow circuit pattern.
Schooling sample. Individuals remain tightly synchronized and change direction as a unit.
Low-mass herbivore with strong group cohesion; record density and spacing rather than single specimens.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.springfi: Compact, high-mobility specimen that stores energy in a coiled posture.
The species displays abrupt jumps and resists prolonged restraint, so handling windows are short.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.swirl_ma: Current-distorting specimen. Water flow becomes unstable before direct contact is made.
The organism sustains a local vortex pattern with minimal movement, which complicates navigation.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.tripod.p: Three-point titan specimen. Its balance is unusual and remains stable under load.
Motion is deliberate and mechanically regular, suggesting a structure optimized for sustained movement.
block.aquanaut.dissection_table.tooltip: Table sections placed side by side merge into a 2x1 bench, and a 2x2 square into a full dissection bench.
block.aquanaut.investigation_board.toolt: A wall-mounted evidence board for organizing field notes and specimens.
Field observation records a ribbon of pale muscle threading the dark, and a faint metallic note in the water before it is seen at all.
The jaw is a sucker ring lined with recurved fangs. It feeds on air as much as on flesh — divers report the gauge falling faster than the wound explains.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.oresucke: Logged repeatedly beside mineral outcrops, its snout worn smooth by grinding.
Stomach contents were pure ore grit. It does not hunt: it eats the rock and keeps the metal, and a patient hunter can recover what it swallowed.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.flagello: A coiled shell drifting against the current, holding more segments than any nautilus should.
The shell is a spring. When pressed, the whorl releases and the whole assembly lashes out like a whip; the siphon then carries it clear before a second strike is possible.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.skeleton: Bare ribs and a working tail. By every measure we have, it should not be swimming.
Damage assessment: the skeletal frame re-knits after impact. Field note — do not assume the first kill is final.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.golden_c: A flash of gold inside the silver shoal; the school parts around it without being asked.
The flesh holds a faint eudaimonic charge. Carrying one is reported to bend chance, and the specimen itself appears entirely unaware of this.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.silver_c: A shoal moving like a single sheet of polished metal.
The flash is defensive: light bounces off the scales in a hard glint that blinds whatever struck first, then the shoal breaks apart in every direction.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.gentlefi: It approached without fear, tipped its hat and withdrew to a polite distance.
Observed habit: it collects dropped items and returns them to divers. Feeding behaviour is orderly to the point of inefficiency.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.slimmy.p: The water thickened to a slick around it, and contact left slime in every seam of my gear.
A bag of lubricant with fins: almost no drag, no aggression at all, and a handling cost of one bottle of cleaner.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.ionfin.p: Charge climbs as it circles, and the cage around its core begins to spin up.
The core is a suspended ion cell. Discharge arcs across anything conductive; the fish never calls lightning, but it does not need to.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.opticich: The fish is mostly lens. It holds station forty metres out and paints a thread of light across your chest — that is not a trick of the water, it is ranging.

What it fires is light, not teeth, so it never needs to close. The lance outruns anything you can swim; only cover defeats it. Cut the line while the aperture is still open — do not try to outrun the shot.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.gemini_j: Two bells, one body, and a light inside that changes allegiance.
The specimen alternates between favour and hunger on a fixed cycle. In favour it breathes air into the water around divers; in hunger it runs them down and the pressure sickness follows.
Not a fish — a drifting reef. Coral grows from its back and small life shelters under its bell.
The bell holds a self-sustaining ecosystem: it breathes usable oxygen into the water and seeds seaweed on suitable seabed as it passes. Nothing about it is hostile.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.pale_aby: A pale boulder on the trench floor, until the boulder opened.
Eighteen branched arms unfold from a single core. Grabbed divers report pressure sickness and a firm, patient pull inward; it retracts and goes still once the water clears.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.three_he: Three heads on one spine, each scanning a different arc. Backing away sideways is not enough.
The heads bite in sequence, never together: clearing the first jaw can still be met by the second or the third, and one pass resolves as several independent strikes.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.title: INVESTIGATION BOARD
gui.aquanaut.investigation.locked_detail: No reliable field notes yet. Continue exploring to turn this lead into evidence.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.locked_link: The pins align, but the connection has not been supported by evidence.

gui.aquanaut.investigation.controls: Drag empty board to pan  •  Wheel to zoom
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.sunken_s: The habitat did not sink intact. Its western supports were cut cleanly before the pressure hull failed.
Who had access to the external maintenance locks?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.fracture: Cracks radiate inward. The glass was struck from outside, but no impact fragments remain nearby.
What could hit reinforced glass without leaving debris?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.luminous: Blue spores cling to the wreck and pulse every eleven seconds. They are absent from the surrounding reef.
Are the pulses a signal, a response, or a warning?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.last_log: The recovered recorder contains forty-three seconds of distorted sonar and one spoken coordinate.
Why was the evacuation order overwritten?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.abyssal_: A repeating carrier rises from below charted depth. Its interval matches the spores found at K-17.
Is something below the trench answering the station?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.node.silent_t: Life vanishes along a narrow route into the trench. Even passive hydrophones go quiet at its boundary.
What is suppressing both wildlife and instrumentation?
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.impact.d: The station's displacement and the viewport fracture point to the same north-west approach vector.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.sample.d: Every spore sample was collected from fresh metal exposed when K-17 broke apart.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.timestam: The viewport failed seven seconds before the final recorder entry, placing the sound inside the attack window.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.frequenc: Filtering the last log reveals the same eleven-second interval now transmitting from abyssal depth.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.migratio: Spores appear along the edge of the lifeless corridor, as though carried outward from the trench.
gui.aquanaut.investigation.link.coordina: The last intelligible coordinate in K-17's log resolves to the silent trench boundary.
gui.aquanaut.water_world.screen.descript: A world of nothing but deep ocean and Aquanaut's own seas: beneath the waves lie coral forests, jelly jungles, brine mirror gorges, brimstone calderas, crystal nests and the middle-level ocean, layer upon layer.
gui.aquanaut.water_world.screen.hint: Select "Water World" as the world type and create the world to dive in.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.ambush_f: The specimen disappears against sediment until a close approach triggers a sudden escape burst.
Its flattened body and muted pattern are specialized for concealment on mud and sand beds.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.garden_e: A group of narrow bodies rises from the sediment and moves only with the surrounding current.
The colony retreats below the seabed when disturbed, leaving almost no trace above the mud.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.hermit_c: This shell-bearing scavenger patrols sediment edges and keeps close to abandoned shell piles.
When threatened it withdraws behind its shell; larger shells appear after repeated access to shell deposits.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.mud_silv: The parasite emerges from compromised mud and immediately searches for a living host.
Bright light interrupts its pursuit, confirming that the species is adapted to buried, low-light sediment.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.sediment: The seabed shifts without warning, and a segmented body lunges out from the disturbed mud.
It retreats below the surface after a single strike, waiting for the next careless footstep.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.humus_je: A pale bell drifts above the humus layer, trailing threads through the murky water.
When struck it bursts into a cloud of organic particles, briefly hiding everything around it.
gui.aquanaut.notebook.waterlife.ancient_: A living fossil drifts slowly near exposed fossil beds, its heavy spiral shell layered with sediment.
Threatened, it withdraws entirely into the shell and waits for the danger to pass.
